q: Which of these is a testable hypothesis?
options: Weekend records have a higher average revenue than weekday records
why: A testable hypothesis names a measurable quantity and a comparison that data could contradict.

options: There is a 97% chance the effect is real
If there were truly no difference, a gap this large would appear about 3% of the time
There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
why: A p-value is about the data given no effect. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about size.

q: Which test suits comparing the means of two groups whose spread (variance) differs?
why: Welch's t-test does not assume equal variances. A paired test needs matched pairs; chi-square is for counts.

q: You slice the data into 20 segments and one shows p = 0.04. What is the concern?
options: With 20 tests you expect about one false positive by chance alone
Segments always have a lower p-value
why: Multiple comparisons inflate false positives. Correct for it, or treat the segment as a lead to confirm on new data.

q: Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together. The most likely explanation is:
options: Sunburn makes people buy ice cream
A confounder, hot sunny weather, drives both
why: Correlation is not causation. Look for a third variable that moves both.

q: You backtest forecast methods by hiding the last 3 points. Why not just score each method on the data it was fitted to?
options: A flexible method can fit the past almost perfectly and still forecast badly
The metrics only work on new data in Python
why: A backtest scores forecasts of data the method never saw, which is what you need from it. In-sample fit rewards overfitting.

q: Your data is two clusters, around 10 and around 30. Which summary is the most misleading?
why: A bimodal sample is usually two groups mixed. The overall mean sits where almost no values are; split the groups first.

q: What should come first in a data science project?
options: A one-sentence question and the decision it serves
Collecting every dataset you can find
why: The question decides which data, method and result you need. Starting with the data or the model usually answers a question nobody asked.

q: A free-text 'notes' column in your data holds the reason customers leave. How should you treat it?
options: Ignore it because it is not numeric
Treat it as unstructured data that may explain the numbers, and plan how to use it
Delete it to keep the table clean
Convert it to a number by counting letters
why: Unstructured text often holds the 'why' behind a number. Decide whether and how to use it rather than throwing it away.

q: Roughly how much of a data project is usually spent preparing the data?
why: Preparation (cleaning, joining, building the outcome and features) is the longest step. Skipping it sends you back to the start.

q: Why check that a join key is unique before you join?
options: Unique keys make the query faster
A repeated key multiplies rows and inflates sums and counts
why: With a repeated key each row matches several rows on the other side, so totals are counted more than once.

q: regexp_replace(col, 'a', 'b') changed only the first 'a' in each value. What fixes it?
why: Without the global flag the function replaces only the first match. In DuckDB: regexp_replace(col, 'a', 'b', 'g').

q: Two variables have a correlation of 0.8. What can you conclude?
options: They tend to move together, which does not show cause
One is a copy of the other
why: Correlation measures association. Cause needs a design that separates it from other explanations.

q: Why compare a model to a baseline on held-back data?
options: To see whether it beats a simple guess on rows it has never seen
To remove the need for a test set
why: A model that cannot beat the baseline on unseen data adds nothing, and its training score only measures memory.

q: A missed case costs far more than a false alarm. Which setting suits you?
options: Favour catching more positives, accepting more false alarms
why: Choose the cut-off by the cost of each kind of mistake. When misses are expensive, accept extra false alarms to catch more.

q: What is a sensible way to roll out a new model?
options: Pilot with a small group, with training and a way to see problems early
Hand over the file and leave
why: A pilot limits the damage of surprises, and training plus feedback make sure people can actually use the result.

q: Sales rose after your model launched. What should you check before crediting it?
options: Whether something else changed (season, price, promotion) or whether a comparison group exists
why: Before and after is not proof of cause. Compare with a group that did not get the change, or rule out other explanations.

q: What does a good write-up allow a non-technical reader to do?
options: Repeat the conclusion correctly and know the recommended action
why: The test is whether someone who skips the maths can state the conclusion and act on it.
